items.originalTitle: China's open-weights AI strategy is winning
items.summary:
China is advancing its AI strategy by releasing open-weight models that can be used and modified freely, contrasting with the proprietary approach of US companies. This openness allows Chinese models to integrate widely across sectors, turning US export restrictions on GPUs into a distribution advantage for China.

While US frontier AI models have historically outperformed open alternatives, Chinese companies like Moonshot and Alibaba now claim competitive models at lower costs, narrowing the performance gap. This shift suggests China’s open approach may foster a more effective global AI ecosystem, challenging US leadership in AI technology and raising questions about future innovation and economic impacts.

items.title: Study finds over 30% of new arXiv papers from 2023 to 2026 exhibit AI-generated writing traits, with computer science leading at 65% and mathematics lowest at 0.7% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Over 30% of new ArXiv submissions now read as AI-written
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed 12,750 arXiv papers from 2021 to mid-2026 using a calibrated AI writing detector designed for academic text. The detector showed a stable 0.4% false-positive rate on pre-ChatGPT papers and identified a rise to about 32% AI-like writing in recent submissions, peaking near 39% in early 2026. The study sampled ten fields monthly, revealing significant variation, with computer science papers most flagged and mathematics papers least, though the latter's results may reflect detector limitations rather than low AI use.

The detector assesses whether text reads as machine-written but cannot distinguish between lightly edited and fully AI-generated content, so the reported figures represent a lower bound on AI writing prevalence. Limitations include small control samples per field and varying detector sensitivity across disciplines. The findings highlight increasing AI involvement in academic writing but do not attribute authorship or intent.

items.originalTitle: Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8, and Anthropic's (Potential) Unravelling
items.summary:
Moonshot Labs and Alibaba recently released two state-of-the-art foundation models, Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8, which reportedly approach the performance of Anthropic's Fable 5 and will have their model weights publicly available soon. These launches highlight a strategic challenge to leading model developers, demonstrating that top-tier performance is achievable with open models and potentially threatening Anthropic's product differentiation.

The article analyzes the economics of foundation model development, emphasizing the high costs of training and inference, and how ownership of infrastructure like data centers and power generation affects margins. Companies owning more of the infrastructure stack can better monetize their offerings, while those relying on leased resources face tighter margins and must compete primarily on model quality or cost. Anthropic's focus on regulatory strategy and recursive self-improvement places it in a precarious position, especially given its models' higher inference costs compared to competitors. The evolving landscape suggests increased competition and potential price pressures in the foundation model market.

items.originalTitle: Launch HN: Bloomy (YC S26) – AI-powered mastery learning for K-12
items.summary:
Bloomy, a startup founded by a former teacher, has launched an AI-driven mastery learning platform for K-12 students that diagnoses skill gaps, creates personalized learning paths, and provides standards-aligned lessons with an interactive AI tutor. The platform aims to replicate the benefits of one-on-one tutoring by using AI to scaffold learning without simply giving answers, helping students achieve mastery before advancing.

The system integrates third-party assessments and its own diagnostics to tailor learning paths, with each skill divided into three stages: concept introduction, guided practice with AI support, and an independent mastery assessment. BloomyBot, the AI tutor, offers scaffolded assistance based on student responses and adapts to their needs while restricting help during assessments to ensure genuine mastery. The platform supports multiple languages and emphasizes collaboration with teachers and parents rather than replacing them.

items.title: Yang AI Lab launches Inertia-1, a unified motion foundation model pretrained on wrist accelerometry and adaptable across body placements and sensor types [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Inertia-1: An Open Exploration to a Unified Motion Foundation Model
items.summary:
Inertia-1 is an open exploration toward a general motion model that unifies diverse datasets and tasks under one framework. It is pretrained on over 18 million hours of wrist accelerometry data using self-supervision and can adapt to different body placements, sensor modalities, and sampling rates with minimal or no retraining. The model aims to power a wide range of applications from fitness tracking to clinical screening by providing a consistent representation of human motion.

The project highlights key sensing design principles such as the benefits of full triaxial input, optimal window lengths of 30–60 seconds, and the advantages of time-domain modeling for preserving gait and health signals. Inertia-1 also supports stacking multiple sensor streams like gyroscope and magnetometer data to improve accuracy and signal clarity. This initiative invites collaboration from researchers and practitioners interested in advancing motion understanding across varied contexts and devices.

items.title: Georgia Power uses eminent domain to seize hundreds of homes for $16B AI data center power expansion, affecting Coweta and Fayette counties
items.originalTitle: Georgia residents homes seized by private company in $16B AI data center plan
items.summary:
Georgia Power, a Southern Company subsidiary, is seizing hundreds of properties in Georgia through eminent domain to build a 35-mile transmission corridor supporting a $16 billion plan to add 10 gigawatts of power capacity, primarily for AI data centers. The project, called Project Wansley, will demolish 20 to 30 homes and place high-voltage power lines near many others, sparking protests from affected residents.

Homeowners like Ansley Brown and Cynthia Van Epps report low compensation offers and forced easements that significantly reduce property value and usability. The utility's expansion aims to meet surging electricity demand driven by AI infrastructure, but residents question the fairness of the process and the long-term impact on their communities and property taxes.

items.title: Report: Ontario's AI-based SAFER system assigns Black prisoners harsher security levels, leading to more restrictive conditions amid racial bias concerns [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Ontario prison AI assigns black prisoners harsher living conditions
items.summary:
Ontario's jails have used the AI-driven Security Assessment for Evaluating Risk (SAFER) program since 2021 to assign prisoners to security levels based on risk scores. A class action lawsuit alleges that SAFER disproportionately assigns Black prisoners to harsher living conditions, such as maximum security, due to biased input data reflecting systemic racism in policing and courts. The Ministry of the Solicitor General acknowledged systemic discrimination affecting Indigenous and racialized inmates but has only implemented measures to reduce Indigenous prisoners in maximum security, not Black prisoners.

The lawsuit highlights that Black individuals, who make up 5.4% of Ontario's population, represent nearly 27% of maximum-security inmates, with Black women particularly affected. Prisoners in higher security levels face more restrictive environments and limited access to visits and programs. Critics argue that the province's continued use of SAFER without adjustments for Black prisoners violates their Charter rights by denying equal protection and benefit under the law.

The Ministry of the Solicitor General acknowledged systemic discrimination affecting Indigenous and racialized inmates but has only implemented measures to reduce Indigenous prisoners in maximum security, not Black prisoners.

The lawsuit highlights that Black individuals, who make up 5.4% of Ontario's population, represent nearly 27% of maximum-security inmates, with Black women particularly affected. Prisoners in higher security levels face more restrictive environments and limited access to visits and programs. Critics argue that the province's continued use of SAFER without adjustments for Black prisoners violates their Charter rights by denying equal protection and benefit under the law.

items.originalTitle: AI makes people confidently wrong
items.summary:
New research from universities in France and Italy reveals that access to AI advice significantly lowers users' accuracy—from 27% to 9%—while increasing their confidence from 30% to 76%. This phenomenon, termed fluency-based substitution, causes people to accept AI-generated answers without verification, reducing their willingness to admit uncertainty and leading to overconfidence in incorrect information.

The study highlights a workplace trend where individuals rely heavily on AI outputs, often producing lengthy but inaccurate content they believe to be their own work. This behavior, described as the rise of "slop zombies," can decrease overall team productivity by spreading unverified and misleading information. The findings underscore the importance of maintaining critical evaluation skills when interacting with AI-generated content to avoid cognitive surrender and misinformation.

There is little question that Moonshot’s Kimi K3 is impressive. The largest open-source model in the world, with 2.8 trillion parameters, it performed impressively on some AI benchmarks, topping a key coding leaderboard from Arena, for instance—ahead of both OpenAI‘s GPT-5.6 and Anthropic’s most powerful model, Claude Fable 5. 

Anastasios Angelopoulos, co-founder and CEO of Arena, said in an interview on The Information's TITV that Kimi K3 challenges the perception that Chinese open-source models are advancing simply by learning from top U.S. models, a process known as distillation. 

“This is the first time we're really seeing the narrative that breaks that mental model, that says that the Chinese labs might actually just be really good at developing models and not just distilling American intelligence,” Angelopoulos said.

items.summary:
Adobe has updated its experimental Indigo camera app, originally designed to provide a natural, SLR-like look for iPhone photos, by integrating a suite of generative AI editing tools. The new "AI Playground" features include AI-generated filter effects, object removal, photo feedback, and custom edits, powered initially by Google's Nano Banana AI model rather than Adobe's own Firefly models. This update is being tested with a small group of users and offers an opt-out option to retain the original app experience.

The AI Playground includes four main sections: Styles for preset filter effects, Object Editing for removing unwanted elements from photos, Photo Guidance for AI-based feedback on shots, and Custom Edit for detailed image manipulation via prompts. Adobe describes this as an experimental phase to learn user interaction with generative AI editing, with potential plans for a paid version if successful. The company is also working on adding metadata standards for AI content transparency to images edited with these tools.

items.summary:
AI Mania Is Eviscerating Global Decision-Making

Here's an entertaining perspective from Nik Suresh on the AI mania that is overwhelming the large companies that he consults with. It's crammed with spicy anecdotes from anonymous sources.

In one extreme case, I have seen an executive confess that they had never even used ChatGPT or any AI tool in their life, immediately after producing a technical strategy for an organisation with $2B+ in revenue which was entirely centered around AI.

Here's a report from an engineer at a company with a token leaderboard:

Checking out a parallel copy of our Go repository and telling the AI to rewrite the whole thing in Zig while I work on something else just so I can keep my job.

I particularly enjoyed this conversation with a skeptical executive at an over-enthusiastic company:

I asked why this was being repeated without opposition. Was it just sales fluff?

The answer was a lot more interesting. It was partially ridiculous sales material being delivered to an easily excitable audience, but this was not the dominant factor constraining honesty. Executives at their customers were saying absurd things about achieving 100x productivity, and this meant that if any executive at the vendor said that these gains were not plausible, it would undermine the credibility of the customer’s executive, be perceived as an attack (or heresy), and possibly result in an enterprise contract cancellation. And getting enterprise contracts cancelled because you wanted to opine on something that doesn’t really matter to your organisation’s mission is a great way to get fired.

Via Hacker News

items.title: Claude Code uses Bun written in Rust now [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Code uses Bun written in Rust now
items.summary:
In Rewriting Bun in Rust Jarred Sumner made the following claim:

Claude Code v2.1.181 (released June 17th) and later use the Rust port of Bun. Startup got 10% faster on Linux but otherwise, barely anyone noticed. Boring is good.

I decided to have a poke at my own Claude Code installation to see if I could find evidence that it was using Bun written in Rust.

I found these two commands convincing:

strings ~/.local/bin/claude | grep -m1 'Bun v1'

For me this outputs Bun v1.4.0 (macOS arm64). The most recent release of Bun on GitHub is currently v1.3.14 from May 12th, so that v1.4.0 version number in Claude supports them shipping a preview of a not-yet-released Bun version.

(Update: The Rust version has been released as Bun canary - running bun upgrade --canary will install this release.)

strings ~/.local/bin/claude | grep -Eo 'src/[[:alnum:]_./-]+\.rs'

This outputs a list of 563 filenames, starting with these:

src/runtime/bake/dev_server/mod.rs src/runtime/bake/production.rs src/bundler/bundle_v2.rs

It looks like Bun in Rust is indeed being run in production across millions of different devices. Like Jarred said, "Boring is good".

Update: Here's a neat trick from Ajan Raj:

cat > /tmp/bun-version.ts <<'EOF' console.log("embedded bun:", Bun.version); process.exit(0); EOF BUN_OPTIONS="--preload=/tmp/bun-version.ts" claude --version

This outputs 1.4.0 for me.

Here's the commit from May 17th that updated the version in package.json to 1.4.0. That version hasn't been changed since then, but also hasn't yet made it into a tagged release outside of canary.
